1051.event_title: Canada turns away the passengers of the Komagata Maru
1051.event: The steamship Komagata Maru arrived in Vancouver harbour on 23 May 1914 carrying 376 South Asian passengers who hoped to settle in Canada. Under the immigration laws of the day the government refused almost all of them entry, and after two months aboard the ship was escorted out of the harbour by the Canadian military on 23 July and forced to return to India. In May 2016 Prime Minister Justin Trudeau formally apologised in the House of Commons, saying the Canadian government had been responsible for the laws that kept the passengers out.
1051.explanation: More than a century later the Canadian state accepted that the fault lay with the laws and officials who refused the passengers, not with the people who had come asking to be admitted.
1051.tie_back: The kural says one may ask those whom it is fitting to ask, and if they withhold, the blame is theirs and not the asker's, and Canada's formal apology placed the blame squarely on those who refused.
1051._accuracy_note: Strong fit for blame falling on the one who refuses; the passengers were seeking entry and livelihood rather than alms.

1052.event_title: Beethoven's patrons grant him a lifelong annuity to stay in Vienna
1052.event: When Beethoven was offered the post of music director at the court of Jerome Bonaparte in Kassel, he negotiated with three Viennese patrons, Archduke Rudolph, Prince Lobkowitz and Prince Kinsky, for support that would allow him to remain in Vienna. Their contract, signed on 1 March 1809, guaranteed him 4,000 florins a year, requiring only that he live in Vienna and compose. Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven's pupil, remained his most dependable patron, although the princes' payments were later disrupted by war, death and the devaluation of 1811.
1052.explanation: Beethoven's request was met readily by admirers who considered it an honour to keep him in their city, and for years afterward he was provided for.
1052.tie_back: The kural says that asking itself can be a pleasure when what is asked comes without pain to either side, and Beethoven's patrons gave willingly to keep him as a composer in Vienna.
1052._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: the request was answered gladly, though it was a negotiated arrangement prompted by a rival offer rather than a plea in need.

1053.event_title: Joseph Pulitzer's appeal pays for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal
1053.event: When the American committee raising money for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal ran about 100,000 dollars short and construction stopped, the publisher Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper, the New York World, to ask ordinary readers for small contributions and promised to print the name of every donor. By August 1885 the World had collected more than 100,000 dollars from some 120,000 people, most giving a dollar or less, and the pedestal was completed the following year.
1053.explanation: The appeal turned a stalled project into a shared civic act, with ordinary people proud to see their names in print beside their gift.
1053.tie_back: The kural says that asking of people whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty has a grace of its own, and Pulitzer's public appeal drew an open-handed response from a whole city.
1053._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong fit for dignified asking of willing givers, though the request was for a public monument rather than for personal need.

1054.event_title: Abbe Pierre's winter appeal sets off an uprising of kindness
1054.event: During an exceptionally harsh winter, after learning that a woman evicted from her home had died of cold in a Paris street, the priest Abbe Pierre wrote an appeal for the homeless that was broadcast on Paris-Inter and Radio Luxembourg on 1 February 1954, asking for blankets, tents and stoves. The public response was so great that the press called it an uprising of kindness; within days the government released funds for emergency housing, and the appeal led to the rapid growth of the Emmaus movement.
1054.explanation: A single request on behalf of the destitute was answered so generously that the act of asking became the occasion for an entire nation's giving.
1054.tie_back: The kural says that asking of those who would never withhold, even in a dream, is as honourable as giving, and Abbe Pierre's appeal to a generous public was itself remembered as an act of great charity.
1054._accuracy_note: Strong fit for asking that is as honourable as giving; Abbe Pierre asked on behalf of others rather than for himself.

1055.event_title: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr open Hull-House
1055.event: Inspired by Toynbee Hall in London, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr leased a large house built by Charles Hull in an immigrant district of Chicago in 1889 and moved in to live among their neighbours. They raised money, cared for children, nursed the sick and listened to people in trouble, and by its second year Hull-House was receiving some two thousand people a week, soon adding a public kitchen, kindergarten classes and evening courses.
1055.explanation: Once it was known that Hull-House would not turn people away, the needy of the neighbourhood came to its door in great numbers.
1055.tie_back: The kural says people take up asking only because there are those in the world who never hold back, and the stream of visitors to Hull-House grew precisely because its founders were known to give freely.
1055._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Hull-House offered education and services more than alms, so the link to the kural's point about asking is indirect.

1056.event_title: Operation Manna drops food to the starving Dutch
1056.event: With the occupied western Netherlands starving at the end of the Hunger Winter, the Allies negotiated with the German command so that their aircraft could fly unharmed along agreed corridors. From 29 April 1945 RAF Lancaster bombers flew very low over Dutch drop zones releasing food instead of bombs, and the American Operation Chowhound joined on 1 May; by the German surrender on 8 May the combined missions had dropped more than 10,000 tons of food. Dutch civilians waved at the low-flying aircraft and spelled out messages of thanks in tulips.
1056.explanation: The sight of the bombers arriving with food became one of the most remembered moments of deliverance at the end of the war in Europe.
1056.tie_back: The kural says that the mere sight of givers free from the vice of withholding ends at once all the afflictions of want, and for starving Dutch families the sight of the food planes overhead meant that their ordeal was ending.
1056._accuracy_note: Strong illustration: the arrival of generous givers visibly ended a famine, though relief came through a military operation rather than personal giving.

1057.event_title: Mother Teresa opens Nirmal Hriday for the dying destitute
1057.event: In 1952 Mother Teresa opened Nirmal Hriday, a hospice at Kalighat in Calcutta, for destitute people who were dying and whom many hospitals of the time would not admit. Residents were washed, fed and cared for so that they could die with dignity, and she required workers to respect each person's own religious beliefs; the Nobel Committee later described the dying destitute there as received with warm compassion devoid of condescension.
1057.explanation: Nirmal Hriday became known worldwide for giving the poorest people care without contempt, and it was a central part of the work recognised by the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize.
1057.tie_back: The kural says the heart of the one in need rejoices deep within when givers give without scorn or ridicule, and Nirmal Hriday was founded on giving the destitute care with respect rather than condescension.
1057._accuracy_note: Strong fit for giving without contempt; the sources describe the manner of care rather than the inner feelings of the recipients.

1058.event: The French sociologist and anthropologist Marcel Mauss published Essai sur le don (The Gift) in 1925 in the journal L'Annee sociologique. Comparing forms of exchange in Melanesia, Polynesia and northwestern North America, he examined the religious, legal, economic and mythological sides of giving, receiving and repaying, and argued that such exchanges bind people together through mutual obligation.
1058.explanation: The essay became one of the most influential works in the social sciences, showing that the giving and receiving of gifts is a basic thread of social life rather than a side matter.
1058.tie_back: The kural says that without people who ask, the busy world would be wooden puppets moving to and fro, and Mauss argued that the exchange of giving and receiving is what gives human society its living bonds.
1058._accuracy_note: Next-best: a scholarly work that parallels the kural's idea about giving and receiving rather than a dramatic event.

1059.event_title: Mansa Musa's lavish giving in Cairo spreads his fame
1059.event: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a vast caravan carrying great quantities of gold. In Cairo he met the Sultan of Egypt, and he and his caravan spent and gave away so much gold that its value in Egypt fell for about twelve years afterwards.
1059.explanation: The pilgrimage made Mansa Musa and the wealth of Mali famous across North Africa, the Middle East and Europe.
1059.tie_back: The kural asks what glory givers could have if there were no one to receive, and Mansa Musa's lasting renown as a giver was spread by the many in Cairo who received his gold.
1059._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: fame through giving that depended on recipients, though the sources stress the economic effect more than the receivers.

1060.event_title: Marconi, rebuffed in Italy, takes his wireless to England
1060.event: After his first wireless experiments at his family's estate near Bologna, the young Guglielmo Marconi offered his system to the Italian government, which showed little interest. In 1896 he took his apparatus to England, where William Preece, Engineer-in-Chief of the Post Office, supported his work and he was granted the world's first patent for a system of wireless telegraphy. In 1897 he returned to Italy to give a demonstration to the Italian government at La Spezia.
1060.explanation: Marconi answered a refusal at home by seeking support elsewhere, and he later served Italy in war and diplomacy.
1060.tie_back: The kural says one who asks must not grow angry when refused, and Marconi, turned down by his own government, simply went where help could be had and later came back to demonstrate his invention to it.
1060._accuracy_note: Next-best: the sources document the refusal and his later return, but not his feelings about being refused.
